bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
- **Chinese imports / dumping:** post-QCO-revocation (Nov) import surge compressed margins; QCO/anti-dumping protection removed; future depends on relative China pricing.
- **Polyester spread compression:** near EBITDA-neutral on current spreads; crude/geopolitical volatility (Iran-Israel-US, Strait of Hormuz) the key swing factor.
- **Demand:** downstream destocking/postponement; price-fall fear; weak April-May seasonality + labor migration.
- **MEG/PTA import dependence**, forex (rupee slide, unhedged), logistics/freight, migrant labor availability, recycling plant ramp/client approval execution risk.
bull_bear.title: Risks

bull_bear.body: Candid and conservative. Openly acknowledged "caught on the wrong foot" on forex and that Q4/current spreads are EBITDA-neutral. Chose YoY framing to avoid flattering/misleading QoQ optics. Bullish medium-term ("golden years for polyester once war stops") but refused FY27 firm revenue guidance citing war. Emphasized recycling as differentiated technological moat while staying deliberately conservative on its EBITDA guide.
bull_bear.title: Mgmt tone

bull_bear.body:
- March reported profit flattered by inventory/stock profit; underlying March EBITDA ~neutral.
- Recycling moat = "waste-to-chip" technology, NOT chip-to-yarn (commoditized) — strategy is to **sell chips**, not forward-integrate into yarn (keeps top line lighter but margins/tech-edge concentrated).
- Customers at zero RM inventory → sharp demand snapback risk/optionality once fear clears (INR 8-12/kg spread recovery possible).
- Short-term PTA/MEG duty relief (till June) had limited on-ground impact due to long import cycles.
- Domestic PTA plants initially priced at landed-import parity — savings only emerge once PTA becomes structurally surplus in India.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious

bull_bear.body:
- Capex funded via internal accruals plus structured debt, explicitly with the aim of keeping leverage contained.
- Carries AA- long-term and A1+ short-term credit ratings.
- Strong liquidity and balance sheet allowed the company to hold inventory prudently through the price-normalisation period without compromising ongoing capex commitments.
- Returns have been improving — ROCE 11.76% (FY23) to 14.90% (FY26) and ROE 8.23% to 12.96% over the same period; the deck makes no dividend commentary.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- Fully integrated manufacturing base across chips, POY, FDY, DTY and downstream yarn, described as the source of synergies in its business model
- Scale: capacity grown from 500 TPA in 1994 to over 4,17,240 TPA, positioning it among India's leading PFY producers

- Proprietary in-house R&D in textile-to-textile chemical recycling: DSIR-recognised R&D centre, a granted and published Indian patent, and a 1 MT/day pilot plant operational since 2022
- Captive power and renewable energy base — 12.5 MW solar in Rajasthan, 10.8 MW hybrid wind-solar in Gujarat, rooftop solar at both factories and a 30 MW captive plant, lowering power cost exposure
- Customer qualification with global brands — MoUs signed with Decathlon India and American & Efird Global, LLC for recycled polyester
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Feedstock and crude oil price volatility with limited pass-through — Polyester melt cost rose from around Rs 82 per kg before the Middle East conflict to nearly Rs 106 per kg as paraxylene and MEG prices climbed with Brent moving from about USD 72 to USD 118 per barrel; only part of the increase could be passed on to customers, compressing margins across the polyester value chain. Management states the direction of crude, feedstock availability and freight costs will continue to influence raw material costs and margins during FY27.
- Import dependence on MEG and supply-chain disruption through the Strait of Hormuz — India has adequate domestic PTA capacity but continues to depend heavily on imports for MEG, leaving the industry exposed to supply disruptions and price volatility from the Middle East conflict. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupted crude and LNG supplies and lifted freight and insurance costs; renewed hostilities in July 2026 indicate the risk has not passed.
- Import competition following withdrawal of Quality Control Orders and the lapse of duty exemptions — The withdrawal of Quality Control Orders on polyester yarn and selected feedstocks increased the risk of cheaper imports, while the temporary customs duty exemption on PTA and MEG ended in July 2026 — both raise landed-cost pressure on domestic producers.
- Execution and scale-up risk on the Ecosis chemical recycling project — Management explicitly acknowledges that moving from a successful pilot to reliable commercial production is a significant step; the Rs 300 crore, 27,000 TPA Dahej plant is targeted for commissioning in October 2026 and the industry's experience shows commercial success depends not only on technology but on secure feedstock, committed customers and sustainable project economics. Textile-to-textile recycling is still less than 1% of global fibre production, and India's collection, sorting and processing ecosystem is still evolving.
- Overcapacity and price pressure from upstream feedstock additions — Around 4.1 million tonnes of paraxylene and 2.7 million tonnes of MEG capacity are expected on stream in the second half of calendar 2026. If geopolitical conditions stabilise, easing input costs would also increase competitive pressure on polyester prices, and industry consolidation is expected to continue among smaller and non-integrated producers.
- Single-product and single-activity concentration — Manufacture of man-made fibre accounts for 97.74% of turnover and polyester multifilament yarn alone for 95.86% of total turnover, with only two manufacturing plants (Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Dahej), so earnings track a single product cycle and a narrow site footprint. There are no major customers contributing more than 10% of total revenue, and exports are only 1.56% of turnover, leaving the business heavily geared to the Indian domestic polyester market.
- Currency and demand exposure — Depreciation of the Indian Rupee increased the cost of imports and added pressure on manufacturers dependent on energy and petrochemical feedstocks; India's textile and apparel exports fell 2.2% in US dollar terms in FY26 and export momentum weakened in the second half following changes in the US tariff regime. FY26 also showed that higher polyester prices no longer shift demand to cotton, leaving overall demand weak rather than substituting.
- Regulatory and sustainability compliance transition — Sustainability regulation is shifting from voluntary commitments to mandatory compliance, with the EU formally adopting Extended Producer Responsibility for textiles from 2027-28 and traceability, recycled-content verification and responsible sourcing becoming requirements from global customers. The Company identifies technology advancement, the geo-political environment and stringent regulatory and environmental requirements as having consequential impacts across the value chain that are likely to continue and intensify over time.
- Employee attrition among permanent staff — The permanent-employee turnover rate rose to 36.43% in FY 2025-26 from 20.33% in FY 2024-25 and 23.31% in FY 2023-24, a material step-up in churn even as permanent-worker turnover fell to 10.00%.

outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: During FY26 the Board approved a capital expenditure programme of approximately Rs 690 crore structured around five initiatives spanning capacity, energy, automation and recycling, funded through debt of approximately Rs 335 crore with the balance met from internal accruals. The largest initiative is a textile-to-textile chemical recycling facility at Dahej built through the wholly owned subsidiary Ecosis Limited (formerly Texfil Private Limited) at an estimated project cost of about Rs 300 crore for an annual capacity of 27,000 MT of recycled polyester of virgin-equivalent quality; building construction has started, equipment has been ordered and production is expected to begin by October 2026. The project builds on an in-house R&D programme that began with laboratory research in 2019, was recognised as a DSIR R&D centre in 2020, scaled to a 1 MT/day pilot plant in 2022 with a granted and published Indian patent, and progressed through greenfield commercial plant erection in 2025; MoUs for recycled polyester have been signed with Decathlon India and American & Efird Global, LLC. outlook.body:
- Crude and feedstock direction is the dominant margin driver: Brent rose from around USD 72 per barrel in late February to USD 118 per barrel by year-end after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, lifting paraxylene and MEG costs; polyester melt cost rose from around Rs 82 per kg before the conflict to nearly Rs 106 per kg, only part of which could be passed on.
- Management expects FY27 to be shaped by three factors: the direction of feedstock prices, the pace of recovery in global demand, and the benefits arising from new trade agreements.
- Around 4.1 million tonnes of paraxylene and 2.7 million tonnes of MEG capacity are expected on stream in H2 CY2026 with no significant PTA capacity scheduled; if geopolitics stabilise, feedstock availability should improve, easing input costs but also increasing competitive pressure on polyester prices.
- India has adequate domestic PTA capacity but depends heavily on MEG imports, leaving the industry exposed to Middle East supply disruption and price volatility.
- Domestic demand tailwind: significant new PTA capacities are being established in India, which should reduce import dependence and stabilise the polyester value chain.
- Trade access improving: the India-UK FTA came into force in July 2026, the India-EU agreement is expected operational in 2027, and Indian textile exports now enjoy a modest tariff advantage over China and Vietnam in the US market.
- Policy is mixed: the GST rate reduction on man-made fibres and yarn corrected the inverted duty structure and improved competitiveness, while withdrawal of Quality Control Orders on polyester yarn and selected feedstocks raised the risk of cheaper imports and the temporary customs duty exemption on PTA and MEG ended in July 2026.
- Man-made yarn, fabrics and made-ups was the best-performing major textile export segment in FY26 with 3.6% growth, ahead of readymade garments and cotton textiles; overall India textile and apparel exports grew 2.1% in rupee terms to Rs 3.16 lakh crore but fell 2.2% in US dollar terms.
- Structural opportunity in circularity: recycled polyester is only about 12% of total polyester production and textile-to-textile recycling contributes less than 1% of global fibre production, with nearly 98% of recycled polyester made from post-consumer bottles; bottle-waste availability is tightening as recycled-content mandates spread.
- India generates over 7 million tonnes of textile waste annually, creating a long-term feedstock opportunity for fibre-to-fibre recycling, though collection, sorting and processing ecosystems are still evolving.
- Management expects FY27 to be a year of technology validation, customer qualification and commercial partnerships in textile-to-textile recycling rather than scale.
- Demand substitution has weakened as a lever: FY26 showed that higher polyester prices no longer automatically shift demand to cotton, since energy and freight lifted both fibres simultaneously.
- Industry consolidation is expected to continue, particularly among smaller and non-integrated producers.
- CBAM continues to exclude textiles, polyester and related petrochemical products, providing temporary relief even as brand sustainability expectations rise.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Crude and feedstock direction is the dominant margin driver: Brent rose from around USD 72 per barrel in late February to USD 118 per barrel by year-end after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, lifting paraxylene and MEG costs; polyester melt cost rose from around Rs 82 per kg before the conflict to nearly Rs 106 per kg, only part of which could be passed on.
- Management expects FY27 to be shaped by three factors: the direction of feedstock prices, the pace of recovery in global demand, and the benefits arising from new trade agreements.
- Around 4.1 million tonnes of paraxylene and 2.7 million tonnes of MEG capacity are expected on stream in H2 CY2026 with no significant PTA capacity scheduled; if geopolitics stabilise, feedstock availability should improve, easing input costs but also increasing competitive pressure on polyester prices.
- India has adequate domestic PTA capacity but depends heavily on MEG imports, leaving the industry exposed to Middle East supply disruption and price volatility.
- Domestic demand tailwind: significant new PTA capacities are being established in India, which should reduce import dependence and stabilise the polyester value chain.
- Trade access improving: the India-UK FTA came into force in July 2026, the India-EU agreement is expected operational in 2027, and Indian textile exports now enjoy a modest tariff advantage over China and Vietnam in the US market.
- Policy is mixed: the GST rate reduction on man-made fibres and yarn corrected the inverted duty structure and improved competitiveness, while withdrawal of Quality Control Orders on polyester yarn and selected feedstocks raised the risk of cheaper imports and the temporary customs duty exemption on PTA and MEG ended in July 2026.
- Man-made yarn, fabrics and made-ups was the best-performing major textile export segment in FY26 with 3.6% growth, ahead of readymade garments and cotton textiles; overall India textile and apparel exports grew 2.1% in rupee terms to Rs 3.16 lakh crore but fell 2.2% in US dollar terms.
- Structural opportunity in circularity: recycled polyester is only about 12% of total polyester production and textile-to-textile recycling contributes less than 1% of global fibre production, with nearly 98% of recycled polyester made from post-consumer bottles; bottle-waste availability is tightening as recycled-content mandates spread.
- India generates over 7 million tonnes of textile waste annually, creating a long-term feedstock opportunity for fibre-to-fibre recycling, though collection, sorting and processing ecosystems are still evolving.
- Management expects FY27 to be a year of technology validation, customer qualification and commercial partnerships in textile-to-textile recycling rather than scale.
- Demand substitution has weakened as a lever: FY26 showed that higher polyester prices no longer automatically shift demand to cotton, since energy and freight lifted both fibres simultaneously.
- Industry consolidation is expected to continue, particularly among smaller and non-integrated producers.
- CBAM continues to exclude textiles, polyester and related petrochemical products, providing temporary relief even as brand sustainability expectations rise.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: During FY26 the Board approved a capital expenditure programme of approximately Rs 690 crore structured around five initiatives spanning capacity, energy, automation and recycling, funded through debt of approximately Rs 335 crore with the balance met from internal accruals. The largest initiative is a textile-to-textile chemical recycling facility at Dahej built through the wholly owned subsidiary Ecosis Limited (formerly Texfil Private Limited) at an estimated project cost of about Rs 300 crore for an annual capacity of 27,000 MT of recycled polyester of virgin-equivalent quality; building construction has started, equipment has been ordered and production is expected to begin by October 2026. The project builds on an in-house R&D programme that began with laboratory research in 2019, was recognised as a DSIR R&D centre in 2020, scaled to a 1 MT/day pilot plant in 2022 with a granted and published Indian patent, and progressed through greenfield commercial plant erection in 2025; MoUs for recycled polyester have been signed with Decathlon India and American & Efird Global, LLC. Alongside this, the Company is adding brownfield polyester filament yarn capacity at its existing Dahej unit — POY of 19,800 MTPA, FDY of 28,800 MTPA and DTY of 14,400 MTPA, about 55,000 tonnes per annum in aggregate — at an estimated cost of about Rs 235 crore with commissioning expected in September 2026. A Steam Power Distribution Project will sell around 70 TPH of surplus steam from the 30 MW captive power plant to neighbouring units at an outlay of Rs 85 crore financed through internal accruals, commissioning expected September 2026, and is expected to generate additional EBITDA of around Rs 60 crore annually. A renewable energy investment of about Rs 30 crore, expanding the 10.8 MW hybrid wind-solar project in Gujarat alongside the existing 12.5 MW Rajasthan solar project and rooftop solar at both factories, is expected to raise the captive renewable power share from about 26% to about 55% and save Rs 18 to Rs 20 crore a year. Automation of post-winding operations — auto-doffing and packing across yarn lines — accounts for a further Rs 40 crore. All five projects were described as under implementation at the date of the report.
